lessonPlan.topic: Student Book p.23 - A Listen, point and say

details: Listen, Point and Say checks understanding of word meaning and sound. Listen and point shows they match what they hear to the right image. Say practises first-step pronunciation.
Look for focused listening, accurate pointing to the person with the correct health problem, and clear pronunciation of the new words.

“Achoo! Oh dear I don’t feel well. What can I do? See a doctor? OK, I’ll go. Look! There are so many people here.  Everyone is sick! I'm not sure what's wrong with each person. Can you help me find out?”

Heads Up: 
Focus the students’ attention on the CPT and present relevant features of the language (MFP). Then demonstrate the activity with TA/students.
Heads Down: 
Ss open their books. Instruct and ask ICQs. Then monitor, providing support and stretch where needed. Conduct activity feedback and error correction.
Heads Together: 
Demo/Instruct and ask ICQs, including setting behaviour expectations. Then monitor, providing support and stretch where needed. Conduct activity feedback and error correction.
Reward moment
Check behaviour expectations and reward with APOS or remind for 4Rs

lessonPlan.topic: Student Book p.23 - B. Listen and circle

details: Listen and Circle continues checking sound–image connection. Students practise listening for specific information and clearly circling an image based on what they hear.
Look for careful listening, accurate choices, clear circling, and neat work in students’ books.
“I think the nurse is calling the next patient, but I can't see who it is. Can you listen carefully and circle the person she calls so I know what's happening?”

lessonPlan.topic: Activity Book p.81 - A Unscramble and match

details: Unscramble and match consolidates the spelling and meaning of the target vocabulary. Students reorder the letters to write the words correctly, then match them to the pictures to reinforce comprehension.
Look for accurately spelled words on the lines and correctly drawn lines connecting the words to the corresponding pictures.
“Oh no, the doctor's notes are all scrambled! I can't read what is wrong with these patients. Can you unscramble the words and match them to the pictures to help me fix the notes?”

details: Look at A. Then read and write the letters provides initial practice of the new grammar structure. Students read the dialogues and match them to the correct picture, linking the text to the visual context.

lessonPlan.topic: Student Book p.24 - C. Ask and Answer

details: Ask and answer provides controlled speaking practice of the target question and answer structure. Students role-play asking what is wrong and answering as one of the children in the pictures.
Look for accurate use of “What's the matter?” and “I've got a...”, clear pronunciation of the illnesses, and natural turn-taking between pairs.
“How are you feeling today? Are you sick? I hope not! Maybe you can be a doctor today. I want you to ask your friend, ‘What's the matter?’ and they can tell you what's wrong.”

lessonPlan.topic: Student Book p.24 - D. Roll a die. Then ask and answer. 10m]

details: Roll a die. Then ask and answer provides gamified speaking practice of the target language. Students use a die to select a patient and then practise asking and answering in the third person.
Look for active participation in the game, correct use of the third-person structure “He's/She's got...”, and accurate identification of the illnesses.

“Oh dear I think I’m really sick! I need to go to the hospital. Look at all the people there!  Let's play a game to find out what's wrong with the patients in the windows. Roll the die, find the right person, and ask your friend ‘What’s the matter?’”

The Chant consolidates the target grammar (What's the matter?) and vocabulary (illnesses) through rhythm and repetition. It allows students to practise natural intonation and sentence stress in a fun, high-energy closer.
Look for enthusiastic participation, clear pronunciation of the health problems and questions, and a correct sense of rhythm and intonation from the whole class.

“That was a great game! It sounds like everyone is feeling a little bit sick today, I think you will feel better after a song! Let's finish our lesson with a fun chant about what's the matter with everyone.”
